subject: biology

items.q: Which feature is shared by all 20 of the amino acids that are coded for in the genetic code?
items.correct: An amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and an R-group are all bonded to one alpha carbon atom.
items.misconception: The R-group is identical in every amino acid, and the amine and carboxyl groups are what vary.
items.why: In the generalized diagram the amine and carboxyl groups are drawn out in full with their atoms, while the R-group is a single letter, so students take the fully drawn groups to be the informative, variable parts and the letter R to be a fixed group. R stands for a variable side group: it is the one part of the molecule that is different in each of the 20 amino acids. The amine group, the carboxyl group and the hydrogen on the alpha carbon are identical in all of them, which is why they can be linked into chains by the same reaction.
items.specStatementText: The parts of any amino acid
items.random_wrong: The amine group is bonded directly to the carbon atom of the carboxyl group, with no carbon between.

items.q: Two amino acids react to form a dipeptide. Which statement describes this reaction?
items.correct: The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amine group of the other, and water is released.
items.misconception: A molecule of water is taken in to provide the atoms needed to link the two amino acids together.
items.why: Students confuse condensation with hydrolysis, and the everyday sense of joining things suggests something must be added; in addition, they know that reactions in cells take place in water and assume it must be taking part. In a condensation reaction a hydroxyl group from the carboxyl group and a hydrogen from the amine group are removed and combine to form a molecule of water, which is released. Water is a product of condensation and a reactant only in the reverse reaction, hydrolysis.
items.specStatementText: Condensation makes dipeptides and longer chains
items.random_wrong: The R-group of one amino acid bonds to the R-group of the other, forming the peptide bond between them.

items.q: A polypeptide of 150 amino acids is assembled by condensation reactions. How does the number of water molecules change as the whole chain is formed?
items.correct: 149 released
items.misconception: 150 released
items.why: Students count the units they can see, the amino acids, instead of the joins between them. Some go further and count both functional groups of every amino acid as reacting, forgetting that one peptide bond uses one carboxyl group and one amine group together. Each condensation reaction joins two amino acids with one peptide bond and releases one water molecule. A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds, formed with the release of n − 1 water molecules, because the amine group at one end and the carboxyl group at the other end are left unreacted.
items.specStatementText: Condensation makes dipeptides and longer chains

items.q: What is meant by an essential amino acid?
items.correct: One that cannot be synthesized in the body and must be obtained from food.
items.misconception: One that the body needs in larger quantities than the non-essential amino acids.
items.why: In everyday English essential means important or necessary, so students read the terms as a ranking of importance rather than as a statement about whether the body can make the amino acid itself. All 20 amino acids are needed to build proteins. Essential and non-essential refer to the diet only: essential amino acids cannot be synthesized and must come from food, whereas non-essential amino acids can be made from other amino acids and so do not have to be eaten.
items.specStatementText: Which amino acids must come from food
items.random_wrong: One of the 20 amino acids, all of which must be supplied by the protein in the diet.

items.q: A chemist makes tripeptides using only four different amino acids. Each of the three positions in a chain can hold any of the four amino acids. How many different tripeptides are possible?
items.why: The 20 amino acids are presented as a set, like the letters of an alphabet, and students picture a polypeptide as a rearrangement of that set rather than as a word in which letters can repeat; combinatorics questions at school often involve arranging distinct objects without repetition. Polypeptides can contain any number of amino acids, from a few to thousands, and amino acids can be in any order, including repeats. A chain of 1000 amino acids obviously cannot be made from 20 used once each; it uses many of the amino acids many times.
items.specStatementText: Why the variety of peptide chains is endless

items.q: Why is the number of different possible polypeptides described as effectively infinite?
items.correct: Chains can be of any length, and the 20 amino acids can occur in any order and be used any number of times.
items.misconception: There are very many combinations of amino acids, and the order of the amino acids does not affect the protein.
items.why: Pre-IB courses say that proteins are made of amino acids, and food science describes protein by its amino acid content, so students think of a polypeptide as a mixture of ingredients rather than as a sequence in which position matters. Amino acids can be in any order, and each order is a different polypeptide. The sequence determines how the chain folds, so changing the order changes the shape and the function; this is a large part of why the variety of possible polypeptides is effectively infinite.
items.specStatementText: Why the variety of peptide chains is endless
items.random_wrong: The 20 amino acids can be arranged in any order, but each amino acid can be used only once in a given chain.

items.q: When egg white is heated, its soluble proteins turn into a white solid. What has happened to the protein molecules?
items.correct: Heat has broken the bonds holding their folded shape, so they have unfolded.
items.misconception: Heat has broken the peptide bonds, so the polypeptides have been split into amino acids.
items.why: Students have met peptide bonds as the bonds of a protein and know that digestion breaks proteins into amino acids, so they assume that anything that damages a protein must be breaking the same bonds. Denaturation is a change in shape, not in sequence. Heat and pH changes disrupt the hydrogen bonds and other interactions that maintain the conformation, so the chain unfolds, but the covalent peptide bonds remain intact; the polypeptide is still a polypeptide, only wrongly folded.
items.specStatementText: Heat and pH change a protein's shape
items.random_wrong: Heat has killed the proteins, so they are no longer able to carry out their functions.

items.q: An enzyme's activity at its optimum pH of 7 was 100 units. One sample was placed at pH 2 for 10 minutes, then returned to pH 7: its activity was 4 units after 1 hour and 4 units after 24 hours, and its polypeptide chains were found to be intact. A second sample was cooled to 5 °C for 10 minutes, then returned to 37 °C: its activity was 100 units. What do these results show?
items.correct: The low pH denatured the enzyme, changing its conformation in a way that was not reversed at pH 7, whereas the low temperature did not denature it.
items.misconception: Both treatments denatured the enzyme, but the denaturation caused by cooling was reversed when the sample was warmed again.
items.why: The graph of enzyme activity against temperature falls on both sides of the optimum, and students assume that the same thing, denaturation, explains both falls; the word optimum also suggests that any departure from it is harmful in the same way. Below the optimum, activity is low only because molecules move more slowly and collide less often; the protein keeps its shape and recovers fully when warmed. Above the optimum, increased vibration breaks the bonds holding the conformation, and this denaturation is in most cases permanent. The two sides of the graph have different causes.
items.specStatementText: Heat and pH change a protein's shape
items.random_wrong: The acid-treated enzyme was only temporarily denatured and would have regained full activity if left for longer at pH 7.

items.q: Which statement about the R-groups of amino acids is correct?
items.correct: Hydrophilic R-groups are either polar but uncharged, or charged, and charged R-groups are acidic or basic.
items.misconception: Every hydrophilic R-group must carry a charge; a polar R-group that is uncharged is classed as hydrophobic.
items.why: Students associate attraction to water with ions dissolving, and treat polar and charged as the same category, so an uncharged group seems to them to have nothing for water to be attracted to. Polar R-groups carry partial charges and form hydrogen bonds with water, so they are hydrophilic even though they have no overall charge. The guide's classification is: R-groups are hydrophobic or hydrophilic, and hydrophilic R-groups are polar or charged, the charged ones being acidic or basic.
items.specStatementText: R-groups give proteins their diversity (HL)
items.random_wrong: An acidic R-group carries a positive charge, because an acid is a substance that contains hydrogen ions.

items.q: Thousands of copies of the same enzyme are synthesized in a cell, and every copy has the same three-dimensional shape. Why?
items.correct: The sequence of amino acids, each in its precise position, determines the conformation, so folding is repeatable.
items.misconception: The ribosome and Golgi apparatus mould each polypeptide into the shape the cell needs after it has been synthesized.
items.why: Students learn that proteins are modified in the Golgi apparatus and that the cell controls what happens to them, and they find it hard to accept that a chain folds itself, so they assign the shaping to a cell structure. The sequence of amino acids determines the shape: the R-groups in their precise positions can only form a particular set of bonds, and the chain folds into the conformation those bonds allow. This is why the structure of a protein is precise, predictable and repeatable, and why every molecule with the same sequence folds the same way.
items.specStatementText: Sequence decides shape (HL)
items.random_wrong: Every copy contains the same set of amino acids, and the order in which they occur has no effect at all on the final shape.

items.q: What stabilizes the alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets of a protein's secondary structure?
items.correct: Hydrogen bonds at regular positions between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone.
items.misconception: Hydrogen bonds between the R-groups of amino acids brought close together by folding.
items.why: Students learn the levels of protein structure as a list and the bond types as another list, and they attach every bond to R-groups because R-groups are described as the parts that differ and interact; the regular backbone is not something they have been asked to think about. Alpha helices and beta-pleated sheets are stabilized by hydrogen bonding in regular positions between the C=O group of one peptide bond and the N–H group of another in the backbone. The R-groups project outwards and are not involved; interactions between R-groups belong to tertiary structure.
items.specStatementText: Coils and pleats in the backbone (HL)
items.random_wrong: Disulfide bonds between cysteines spaced at regular intervals along the polypeptide.

items.q: In one region of a polypeptide there are two cysteines, an amino acid whose R-group contains a carboxyl group and an amino acid whose R-group contains an amine group. Which statement about the bonds these could form in the tertiary structure is correct?
items.correct: The cysteines can form a covalent disulfide bond; the carboxyl and amine R-groups can form an ionic bond once the first has lost and the second has bound a hydrogen ion.
items.misconception: The cysteines can form a disulfide bridge, which is a strong hydrogen bond and so is broken by heating as easily as the other hydrogen bonds.
items.why: The four kinds of tertiary-structure interaction are taught together and drawn with the same dotted line in diagrams, so students lump the disulfide bond with the weak interactions and remember only that it is the strongest of them. The disulfide bond is a covalent bond, the only covalent bond among the interactions that hold tertiary structure. It forms between the R-groups of a pair of cysteines, is not broken by moderate heating or by pH changes, and is broken by reducing agents; the other three interactions are weak and non-covalent.
items.specStatementText: Four kinds of bond hold the fold (HL)
items.random_wrong: The carboxyl R-group becomes positively charged and the amine R-group becomes negatively charged, so the two attract and form an ionic bond.

items.q: A soluble globular enzyme was tested. A reducing agent that breaks disulfide bonds cut its activity to 10%. Moving it from pH 7 to pH 4 cut its activity to 30%, and full activity returned when it was moved back to pH 7. Its polypeptide chain stayed intact in both experiments. What do these results show?
items.correct: The tertiary structure depends on disulfide bonds and on ionic bonds between R-groups whose charges change reversibly with pH.
items.misconception: The loss of activity at pH 4 cannot involve ionic bonds, because the charges on R-groups do not change at all when the pH changes.
items.why: Students meet ionic bonding in compounds such as sodium chloride, where the ions have fixed charges, and carry the idea of fixed charges over to proteins without considering where the charge on an R-group comes from. Amine groups in R-groups become positively charged by binding hydrogen ions and carboxyl groups in R-groups become negatively charged by dissociation of hydrogen ions. Raising or lowering the pH changes whether these groups are charged, so ionic bonds between them can be broken and the tertiary structure altered.
items.specStatementText: Four kinds of bond hold the fold (HL)
items.random_wrong: The reducing agent broke hydrogen bonds, since a disulfide bridge is the strongest type of hydrogen bond found in a protein.

items.q: A globular enzyme is dissolved in the cytoplasm, and an integral protein spans the plasma membrane. Where are the amino acids with hydrophobic R-groups located in each protein, and why?
items.correct: In the enzyme's core and the integral protein's membrane region, because water molecules bond to each other and exclude non-polar R-groups.
items.misconception: Absent from the soluble enzyme, because a protein containing hydrophobic amino acids could not dissolve in water.
items.why: Students apply the rule that hydrophobic substances do not dissolve to individual amino acids, treating solubility as the sum of the parts rather than as a property of the folded surface. Solubility depends on what is on the outside. In proteins that are soluble in water, hydrophobic amino acids are clustered in the core of the globular protein, where they are shielded from water and help hold the fold together, and hydrophilic amino acids are on the surface in contact with water.
items.specStatementText: Where polar and non-polar amino acids sit (HL)
items.random_wrong: Throughout the whole of the integral protein, which must be hydrophobic on all of its surfaces to stay in the membrane.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares insulin, collagen and haemoglobin?
items.correct: Haemoglobin is a conjugated protein with haem groups; insulin and collagen are non-conjugated.
items.misconception: All three are conjugated proteins, because each of them is built from more than one polypeptide chain.
items.why: Conjugated proteins are introduced in the same statement as quaternary structure, and haemoglobin is described as having four subunits and four haem groups, so students merge the two ideas and assume conjugated means multi-chain. Conjugation is about composition, not chain number. Haemoglobin is conjugated because each polypeptide carries a haem group, which is not made of amino acids and contains an iron ion. Insulin and collagen also have several polypeptides, but they are non-conjugated because they consist of polypeptides only.
items.specStatementText: Proteins from several polypeptides (HL)
items.random_wrong: The haem groups of haemoglobin are short polypeptides, so all three of these proteins are non-conjugated.

items.q: Cryogenic electron microscopy has produced images of single protein molecules and of their interactions with other molecules. What does this illustrate about the role of technology in science?
items.correct: Technology allows the imaging of structures that would be impossible to observe with the unaided senses, so new knowledge of proteins can be gained.
items.misconception: A light microscope with sufficient magnification could image single protein molecules, so the new technique is simply more convenient.
items.why: Magnification is the quantity students calculate and the property advertised on microscopes, and resolution is rarely calculated, so students explain what a microscope can show by magnification alone. Magnification enlarges the image but does not add detail; resolution sets the smallest separation that can be distinguished. Electron microscopy, including cryogenic electron microscopy, achieves far higher resolution because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, which is what makes imaging of single protein molecules possible.
items.specStatementText: Proteins from several polypeptides (HL)
items.random_wrong: Molecules are far too small for any instrument to image, so protein structures can only be inferred, not observed directly.

items.q: Protein X is compact and roughly spherical, dissolves in blood plasma and binds to a specific receptor on target cells. Protein Y forms long insoluble fibres with high tensile strength in tendons. Which statement correctly relates the form of each protein to its function?
items.correct: X is globular like insulin, its precise shape fitting its receptor; Y is fibrous like collagen, its elongated shape suiting a structural role.
items.misconception: Y is a polypeptide that has not folded up, and its lack of a defined structure is what allows it to form insoluble fibres.
items.why: Globular proteins are described as folded and fibrous proteins as long chains, so students take fibrous to mean unfolded, and picture a fibre as a loose strand rather than as an organized structure. Fibrous proteins are just as precisely structured as globular ones, but their structure is elongated rather than compact. In collagen, each polypeptide is coiled and three of them are wound together into a triple helix; the regular structure is what gives collagen its high tensile strength and insolubility.
items.specStatementText: Globular and fibrous: shape fits job (HL)
items.random_wrong: Y is a single very long polypeptide chain, and its tensile strength comes from the great length of that one chain alone.

items.q: In an amino acid, what is the amine group bonded to?
items.correct: The alpha carbon, which also carries the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group.
items.misconception: The amine group is bonded directly to the carbon of the carboxyl group, so an amino acid is simply an NH₂ group joined to a COOH group.
items.why: Students meet the name amino acid as amine plus acid and write it as NH₂–COOH, leaving out the central carbon; drawings that abbreviate the molecule also make it look as if the two groups are joined to each other. The generalized amino acid has a central alpha carbon with four things attached: the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. The two functional groups are on the same carbon but are not bonded to each other.
items.specStatementText: The parts of any amino acid
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the structure of the amine group of an amino acid?
items.correct: –NH₂: a nitrogen atom bonded to the alpha carbon and to two hydrogen atoms.
items.misconception: The amine group is an NH₃ group, with the same formula as ammonia.
items.why: Ammonia (NH₃) is the nitrogen compound students know best, and a nitrogen atom is usually shown with three bonds to hydrogen, so they carry three hydrogens over to the amine group without noticing that one of nitrogen's three bonds is now to the alpha carbon. In an amine group the nitrogen uses one of its three bonds to attach to the alpha carbon, leaving two hydrogens: –NH₂. The group can bind a hydrogen ion to become –NH₃⁺, but that is a charged form, not the neutral amine group of the generalized structure.
items.specStatementText: The parts of any amino acid
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which parts of two amino acids react to form a peptide bond?
items.correct: The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of the other.
items.misconception: The peptide bond forms between the R-groups of the two amino acids.
items.why: The R-group is presented as the interesting, distinctive part of each amino acid, so students assume it must be the part that does the chemistry when amino acids join; diagrams that draw the R-group large reinforce this. The condensation reaction is between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of the next, forming the peptide bond in the backbone. The R-groups take no part in the reaction and project from the backbone of the finished polypeptide.
items.specStatementText: Condensation makes dipeptides and longer chains
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What type of bond is a peptide bond?
items.correct: A covalent bond between the carbon of a carboxyl group and the nitrogen of an amine group.
items.misconception: A peptide bond is a hydrogen bond, because it involves the N–H of the amine group.
items.why: Hydrogen bonds are the bond type most often discussed in connection with proteins and other biological molecules, and the peptide link contains an N–H group, so students assume the link itself is a hydrogen bond. The peptide bond is a covalent C–N bond formed by condensation; it is strong and is not broken by heating or by changes in pH. Hydrogen bonds do occur in proteins, but between C=O and N–H groups of different peptide bonds or between R-groups, where they help hold the folded shape.
items.specStatementText: Condensation makes dipeptides and longer chains
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all 20 amino acids have to be obtained from food?
items.correct: No. Only the essential amino acids must come from food; the non-essential amino acids can be made in the body from other amino acids.
items.misconception: The body cannot make amino acids, so every amino acid it uses has to come from digesting protein in food.
items.why: Pre-IB courses teach that protein in food is digested to amino acids that the body uses to build its own proteins, without mentioning that the body can also convert one amino acid into another, so students see food as the only source. Non-essential amino acids can be synthesized from other amino acids, so they need not be present in the diet. It is only the essential amino acids that cannot be synthesized and must be obtained from food.
items.specStatementText: Which amino acids must come from food
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many different tripeptides can be made from the 20 amino acids if any amino acid can be used at each position?
items.correct: 20 × 20 × 20 = 20³ = 8000, because each of the three positions can independently hold any of the 20.
items.misconception: The number of possible sequences is found by multiplying, adding, or otherwise combining the number of amino acids with the chain length, rather than by raising the number of amino acids to the power of the chain length.
items.why: Students have not met the idea that independent choices multiply, so they reach for the simplest arithmetic that uses the two numbers in the question, such as 20 × 3 or 20 + 20 + 20, or they put the numbers the wrong way round and calculate 3²⁰. Each position in a chain is an independent choice from the 20 amino acids, so the number of sequences is 20 multiplied by itself once for each position: 20ⁿ for a chain of n amino acids. This grows so fast with chain length that the variety of possible polypeptides is effectively infinite.
items.specStatementText: Why the variety of peptide chains is endless
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does a denatured enzyme no longer work?
items.correct: Because its three-dimensional shape has changed, so the active site no longer fits its substrate; the protein is a molecule, so it cannot be alive or dead.
items.misconception: Heat kills enzymes and other proteins, which is why they stop working.
items.why: Everyday language says that heat kills germs and that enzymes are killed by boiling, and students transfer the word to proteins without noticing that only organisms can be killed. Proteins are molecules, not living things. When a protein is denatured its conformation changes and it loses its function because the shape that made the function possible has been lost; describing this as killing hides the real mechanism, which is the breaking of the bonds that maintain the shape.
items.specStatementText: Heat and pH change a protein's shape
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If a protein is denatured by heat or by an extreme pH, does it return to its original shape when normal conditions are restored?
items.correct: In most cases no: the unfolded chains are unlikely to refold correctly, so denaturation is usually permanent.
items.misconception: Denaturation is a temporary change: once the temperature or pH returns to normal the protein folds back into its original shape and works again.
items.why: Students learn that a protein's shape is determined by its sequence, and reason that if the sequence is unchanged the shape must come back; they also generalize from the reversible effect of low temperature, where activity does return. Denaturation is in most cases permanent. Once the bonds holding the conformation are broken, the unfolded chains interact with each other in new ways and do not usually find their way back to the original shape when conditions are restored, as the solid white of a cooked egg shows.
items.specStatementText: Heat and pH change a protein's shape
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do hydrophobic R-groups end up away from water?
items.correct: Because water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and not to non-polar groups, so the non-polar groups are excluded from the water and cluster together.
items.misconception: Hydrophobic R-groups actively repel water molecules and push them away.
items.why: The word hydrophobic means water-fearing, and everyday descriptions say that oil and water repel each other, so students picture a repulsive force between the R-group and water. There is no repulsion. Non-polar groups simply cannot form hydrogen bonds, so water molecules bond with each other instead and the non-polar groups are left to associate with one another; these hydrophobic interactions are a consequence of the attraction between water molecules, not of a force pushing water away.
items.specStatementText: R-groups give proteins their diversity (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What determines the properties of an assembled polypeptide?
items.correct: The R-groups of its amino acids: their chemical diversity is the basis of the diversity of protein form and function.
items.misconception: The properties of a polypeptide come from its amine and carboxyl groups, which every amino acid has, so the R-groups have little influence.
items.why: The generalized diagram draws the amine and carboxyl groups in full and reduces the R-group to a letter, and the condensation reaction students study involves only the amine and carboxyl groups, so these seem to be the chemically important parts. Once amino acids are linked, their amine and carboxyl groups are used up in peptide bonds and form a repeating backbone that is the same in every polypeptide. It is the R-groups projecting from that backbone, hydrophobic or hydrophilic, polar or charged, that determine how the chain folds and what it can do.
items.specStatementText: R-groups give proteins their diversity (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What charge does an acidic R-group carry when it is ionized?
items.correct: A negative charge: its carboxyl group dissociates, releasing a hydrogen ion and leaving –COO⁻.
items.misconception: An acidic R-group is positively charged, because acids contain hydrogen ions, and a basic R-group is negatively charged.
items.why: Students link the word acid with H⁺ and so with positive charge, without following through that an acid gives its hydrogen ion away and is left negative; the everyday pairing of acid with positive and base with negative feels natural. A carboxyl group in an R-group is acidic because it can dissociate to release a hydrogen ion, which leaves the R-group negatively charged. An amine group in an R-group is basic because it can bind a hydrogen ion, which makes the R-group positively charged. Oppositely charged R-groups of these two kinds can then form ionic bonds.
items.specStatementText: R-groups give proteins their diversity (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the identity of an amino acid far from a protein's active site affect the protein's shape?
items.correct: Yes. The precise position of every amino acid contributes to the conformation, so a change anywhere in the sequence can alter the shape.
items.misconception: Only the amino acids that form the active site matter; changing an amino acid elsewhere in the sequence does not affect the protein's shape.
items.why: Pre-IB enzyme teaching focuses entirely on the active site, and diagrams show the rest of the enzyme as a featureless blob, so students conclude that the remainder of the sequence is filler. The whole sequence determines the conformation, because bonds between R-groups throughout the chain hold the fold together. An amino acid substitution far from the active site can change the folding and so change the shape of the active site indirectly, which is why proteins have precise and repeatable structures only when the sequence is exact.
items.specStatementText: Sequence decides shape (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an integral membrane protein hydrophobic throughout?
items.correct: No. It has regions with hydrophobic R-groups that embed in the bilayer, and regions with hydrophilic R-groups that project into the aqueous solutions on either side.
items.misconception: An integral protein must be hydrophobic all over in order to stay in the membrane.
items.why: Students learn that the membrane interior is hydrophobic and that like dissolves in like, and conclude that anything in the membrane must be uniformly hydrophobic; diagrams drawing integral proteins as a single blob do not show separate regions. Integral proteins have regions with hydrophobic amino acids, which sit in the hydrophobic centre of the bilayer and anchor the protein, but the parts that extend into the cytoplasm or the extracellular fluid have hydrophilic R-groups. A protein hydrophobic all over could not function in contact with water.
items.specStatementText: Where polar and non-polar amino acids sit (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does insulin have quaternary structure?
items.correct: Yes. Insulin consists of two polypeptides linked by disulfide bonds, so it has quaternary structure although it is a small protein.
items.misconception: Insulin is a single short polypeptide, so it has tertiary structure but no quaternary structure.
items.why: Insulin is introduced as a small hormone and is often drawn as one compact blob, and students assume that quaternary structure belongs only to large proteins such as haemoglobin. Insulin is made of two polypeptides, of 21 and 30 amino acids, held together by disulfide bonds between cysteines, so it has quaternary structure. It is the guide's example of a non-conjugated protein with quaternary structure, alongside collagen with its three polypeptides.
items.specStatementText: Proteins from several polypeptides (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the ribbon and space-filling models of proteins in textbooks based on measurement?
items.correct: Yes. They are drawn from structures determined experimentally, using techniques such as cryogenic electron microscopy and X-ray crystallography.
items.misconception: Pictures of protein structure are artists' impressions worked out from the amino acid sequence, not images of real molecules.
items.why: Protein structures are shown as stylized cartoons with coloured ribbons and arrows, which look like drawings rather than data, and students are told that sequence determines structure, so they assume the pictures were deduced from the sequence. Ribbon diagrams are a way of displaying structures that have been measured. Cryogenic electron microscopy produces images of single protein molecules from which the positions of the atoms are worked out; the cartoon style simplifies the display, but the structure it shows was observed, not imagined.
items.specStatementText: Proteins from several polypeptides (HL)
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the tensile strength of collagen come from?
items.correct: From three polypeptides wound together into a triple helix, with many triple helices linked side by side into fibres.
items.misconception: A collagen fibre is one very long polypeptide, and its strength comes from the length of that chain alone.
items.why: Students picture a fibre as a single thread and know that collagen polypeptides are long, so they equate the fibre with one chain and do not consider how chains are associated with one another. A collagen molecule has quaternary structure: three polypeptides wound around each other, like the strands of a rope. Many of these triple helices are then linked into fibres. It is this winding and cross-linking, not the length of a single chain, that gives tendons, ligaments and skin their resistance to being pulled apart.
